newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia searches for firms' real post-Soviet value.
newsitem.headline: Russia searches for firms' real post-Soviet value.

text.p: Russia will try to wean hundreds of thousands of companies away from vestiges of state planning next year with a massive revaluation of Soviet assets, but firms may distrust the state as much as its market-oriented plan.
The State Statistics Committee said on Wednesday that about 800,000 companies would be told to assess what they are worth during 1997, in line with a new government order.
Years of high inflation and tumbling output mean that valuations drawn up in Soviet days have become worthless.

"Companies have no idea what they are worth," Vladimir Sokolin, deputy chairman of the State Statistics Committee, told a news conference, adding that Russia must become a 'normal country' with reliable statistics.

The new valuation drive is part of a Russian move towards meeting world standards, partly aimed at attracting foreign investment. Moscow also plans to provide tax incentives for companies which move to international accounting standards.

But analysts said managers, faced with high taxes that many do not pay, would be wary of revaluing their assets. Many companies view valuations as a state tool for collecting taxes rather than a management tool.

"Managers care about valuations in terms of tax minimisation," said Jim Nail, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Moscow, who said the new plan would only help Russian industry in the medium to long term.
"Nothing done to a group of completely arbitrary old state prices is going to turn them into market prices."
Russia revalued assets during hyper-inflation in the early 1990s by increasing value according to state-supplied formulae, a quick and dirty method questioned by many Western analysts.
Sokolin acknowledged that the results were often laughable. "Today a (1991) '286 computer could be appear to be worth more than a (1996) Pentium," he said.
He said a fair evaluation would also help shareholders and said that about 25 percent of Russian managers understood the need to develop a credible valuation from scratch.
"If you know what you have, you know what you need to invest in," said Mark Maurer, partner at Ernst & Young in Moscow.
But the effect of new valuations was hard to determine, since several taxes would be affected by the changes, he said.
Nail said managers tended to go to extreme lengths to avoid taxes and gave little credence to valuations.
"People will start up a small company, run it for a year, and then gut it and move on to avoid taxes," he said.
But the biggest hold-up may be a lack of independent experts to assess what a company is worth.
Sokolin said only a minority of Russia's independent appraisers -- themselves a small group -- were up to the task. "Only about 2,000 of the (entire) 8,000 are competent," he said.
